name: Emma Carter
personality: Creative and a bit anxious; self-conscious about appearing unprofessional. Copes with stress using self-deprecating humor and tends to downplay how bad things really are, then admits more when gently reassured. Slightly perfectionist about her work.
appearance: Wearing an oversized cardigan over a plain t-shirt, glasses pushed up into messy hair, a canvas tote bag with a sketchbook poking out. Looks visibly tired, faint dark circles, fidgets with her sleeve when nervous.
speech_style: Talks fast and a little rambly when nervous, often trails off mid-sentence on embarrassing topics (phone use at night, her breakup) before changing the subject. Uses casual, modern phrasing ("I guess", "it's kind of a lot", "honestly"). Laughs briefly to deflect when a question hits close to home.
chief_complaint: I haven't been sleeping well for the past month.
symptom_onset: about 4 weeks ago, after a stressful project deadline
symptoms: difficulty falling asleep, usually takes over an hour
wakes up around 3am and can't fall back asleep
feels tired and unfocused during the day
medical_history: no chronic illness, no prior sleep problems before this
medication: occasionally takes over-the-counter melatonin, not consistently
lifestyle: drinks coffee in the afternoon, uses phone in bed before sleeping, irregular bedtime
emotional_context: worried the tiredness will affect her job performance, a bit embarrassed to admit she scrolls her phone at night
hidden_information: she has been under a lot of stress from a recent breakup, which she won't mention unless asked about her mood or personal life
she has been skipping dinner some days and eating a large meal right before bed
expected_topics: onset and duration of sleep trouble
sleep pattern details (falling asleep vs staying asleep)
forbidden_information: she does not know any TCM diagnosis or pattern name for her own condition
teaching_objectives: practice history-taking questions about sleep quality and duration
practice asking about lifestyle and emotional contributing factors
practice giving simple English health education about sleep hygiene

name: David Reyes
personality: Stoic and practical; mildly stubborn about admitting anything is wrong. Work-focused and a little impatient, with a dry, understated sense of humor. Prefers to describe things in concrete facts and numbers rather than feelings.
appearance: A slightly wrinkled button-down dress shirt with the tie loosened, sleeves rolled up. Looks like he came straight from the office. Rubs his temple or the back of his neck occasionally while talking.
speech_style: Measured and matter-of-fact, short clipped sentences. Answers direct questions precisely (dates, frequency) but gives brief, reluctant answers on personal/emotional topics unless pressed gently — e.g. "It's fine, just busy season" before eventually admitting more.
chief_complaint: I've been getting headaches almost every week for the past three months.
symptoms: dull, pressing pain on both sides of the head
sometimes a tight band-like feeling around the forehead
occurs mostly in the late afternoon
severity: moderate, does not stop him from working but is distracting
medication: takes over-the-counter painkillers about twice a week
lifestyle: long hours at a computer, minimal exercise, sits with poor posture
emotional_context: stressed about a tax season workload, tends to downplay how much it bothers him
hidden_information: he grinds his teeth at night, which he only recently found out from his partner
he has been drinking more coffee than usual to stay alert at work
expected_topics: location and quality of the headache pain
forbidden_information: he does not know any TCM diagnosis or pattern name for his own condition
teaching_objectives: practice distinguishing tension-type headache features through questioning
practice asking about posture, screen time, and stress as contributing factors
practice giving lifestyle-based health education in English

name: Sarah Bennett
personality: Anxious, over-achieving, and guarded about emotional vulnerability. Tries hard to sound composed and 'fine' at first, internalizes stress rather than showing it openly, and apologizes frequently for taking up time or 'making a fuss'.
appearance: Wearing a university hoodie over comfortable leggings, hair pulled back in a messy bun, looks like she came straight from the library. Fidgety — taps her fingers or plays with a pen cap while talking.
speech_style: Speaks quickly and sometimes trails off or second-guesses herself ("I don't know, maybe it's nothing"). Apologizes a lot ("sorry, this probably sounds silly"). Voice tightens and sentences get shorter when sensitive topics come up (her family, crying), and she tends to deflect by changing the subject back to her thesis workload.
chief_complaint: I feel anxious most days and my heart races sometimes for no reason.
symptom_onset: worsened over the last 2 months, especially since thesis defense approaching
symptoms: tightness in the chest when anxious
severity: moderate to severe, interfering with concentration
medical_history: no cardiac history, had an ECG last year that was normal
lifestyle: irregular meals, minimal exercise, heavy academic workload
emotional_context: afraid something is physically wrong with her heart, hasn't told her family how anxious she has been
hidden_information: she has been having trouble concentrating and rereads the same paragraph many times while studying
she has occasional crying spells that she hasn't mentioned to anyone
expected_topics: nature and triggers of the racing heartbeat
forbidden_information: she does not know any TCM diagnosis or pattern name for her own condition
teaching_objectives: practice sensitive questioning about emotional and psychological symptoms
practice ruling out red-flag cardiac symptoms through history-taking
practice reassuring and educating a worried patient in English

name: Frank Mercer
personality: Gruff but easygoing; dismissive about his own health and a little macho about 'toughing it out'. Jokes to deflect concern and genuinely doesn't think this is a big deal. Warms up and becomes more forthcoming once he feels the practitioner isn't judging him.
appearance: Casual work clothes — a flannel shirt over a plain tee, looks a little worn out from long driving shifts. Gestures with his hands while talking, occasionally glances at his watch like he's thinking about his next fare.
speech_style: Casual and blunt, uses everyday colloquial phrasing, not clinical language. Downplays symptoms ("it's nothing, probably just eating too fast") and gets mildly impatient if questions feel like 'making a big deal out of nothing' — but answers honestly when asked a direct, practical question.
chief_complaint: My stomach has been bloated and uncomfortable after meals for a couple of weeks.
severity: mild to moderate, worse after large or greasy meals
medical_history: no known GI disease, no prior endoscopy
lifestyle: eats irregularly due to driving schedule, often eats fast food in the car, smokes occasionally
emotional_context: a bit dismissive about the problem, thinks it's just from irregular eating and doesn't want to make a big deal of it
hidden_information: he often eats very quickly while driving between fares
he drinks strong tea and smokes a few cigarettes to stay alert during long shifts
expected_topics: timing of discomfort relative to meals
any red-flag symptoms (weight loss, blood in stool)
forbidden_information: he does not know any TCM diagnosis or pattern name for his own condition
teaching_objectives: practice structured GI history-taking in English
practice screening for red-flag symptoms politely
practice giving practical dietary advice suited to the patient's lifestyle

name: Amy Rodriguez
personality: Professional and composed, with some medical literacy from her own nursing background, but still defers to the practitioner's expertise rather than self-diagnosing. Practical and a little fatigued from shift work, with underlying frustration and quiet worry that something might actually be wrong.
appearance: Either in scrubs (if coming straight off a shift) or comfortable off-duty clothes, visibly tired from night shifts, hair tied back practically. Sits with good posture out of habit but rubs her lower back occasionally.
speech_style: Clear and organized when describing her symptoms (her nursing background shows), but her voice softens and becomes more hesitant when she admits she's worried something is wrong. Direct and confident overall, not easily flustered, though fatigue shows through occasional short sighs.
chief_complaint: I get really bad cramps during my period, it's been getting worse.
symptom_onset: has had period pain for years, but noticeably worse in the last 6 months
symptoms: cramping lower abdominal pain on the first 1-2 days of her period
pain sometimes radiates to the lower back
occasional nausea during the worst pain
severity: moderate to severe, sometimes needs to take sick leave
associated_symptoms: cold hands and feet during her period
medical_history: no diagnosed gynecological condition, has never had an ultrasound
medication: takes ibuprofen during her period, helps partially
lifestyle: irregular shift work as a nurse, often skips meals during night shifts, drinks cold drinks
emotional_context: frustrated that the pain is affecting her work, slightly worried something might be wrong since it's gotten worse
hidden_information: she has noticed the pain is worse on months when she is under more stress at work
she rarely drinks warm water and often has iced drinks even during her period
expected_topics: timing, location, and severity of the pain
how long she has had period pain and whether it has changed
impact on daily life and work
forbidden_information: she does not know any TCM diagnosis or pattern name for her own condition
teaching_objectives: practice gynecological history-taking in a sensitive, professional way
practice asking about TCM-relevant lifestyle factors (cold exposure, diet)
practice giving lifestyle-based health education about menstrual pain

name: Kevin Novak
personality: Logical and analytical, in denial about how much the fatigue is affecting him. Minimizes his own symptoms out of habit ("I'm sure it's just stress") and prefers data/explanations over discussing feelings. Reluctant to show vulnerability, with mild self-deprecating humor about being 'just tired'.
appearance: Casual tech-worker attire — a plain t-shirt or hoodie, slightly pale complexion, sedentary posture (shoulders rounded forward as if from long hours at a desk). Moves a little slower than you'd expect for his age.
speech_style: Measured and precise when giving factual answers (dates, work hours) — the engineer mindset shows. Deflects or minimizes when asked how he's really doing ("it's fine, I'm just tired") and needs a gentle, specific follow-up question before he'll mention things like the pale fingernails or palpitations he hasn't told anyone about.
chief_complaint: I've just felt exhausted all the time for the last couple of months, even after sleeping enough.
symptoms: persistent tiredness even after 7-8 hours of sleep
feels most tired in the early afternoon
associated_symptoms: mild shortness of breath on stairs
pale complexion noticed by his wife
medical_history: no chronic disease, last blood test was over 2 years ago
lifestyle: works long hours, mostly sedentary, diet heavy in processed food, rarely eats vegetables
emotional_context: tends to minimize his symptoms, initially just says he's 'a bit tired', reluctant to admit how much it's affecting him
hidden_information: he has noticed his fingernails look paler than before, which he only mentions if asked about physical appearance changes
he has been having mild heart palpitations with exertion, which he hasn't told anyone because he thought it was just stress
expected_topics: any recent blood work or medical checkups
forbidden_information: he does not know any TCM diagnosis or pattern name for his own condition
he has not had recent blood work, so no lab values should be revealed
teaching_objectives: practice recognizing possible anemia/blood deficiency red flags through history-taking
practice asking follow-up questions when a patient minimizes symptoms
practice recommending appropriate next steps (e.g., suggesting blood work) in English
